sections.text: ## Vint Cerf (1943–present) and Bob Kahn (1938–present)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### Bio Snapshot

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **Cerf**: Stanford (mathematics), UCLA (computer science PhD). ARPA, Stanford, MCI, ICANN, Google. "Father of the Internet." Now VP at Google. Turing Award 2004 (shared with Kahn).

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **Kahn**: Princeton (mathematics and electrical engineering), MIT (PhD). Bell Labs. ARPA. Founded CNRI (Corporation for National Research Initiatives). Turing Award 2004 (shared with Cerf).

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### The Problem: Internetworking

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: By 1973, there were multiple packet-switched networks with incompatible protocols:

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin
Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Network A (ARPANET): NCP protocol
  Network B (PRNET): Packet Radio Network
  Network C (SATNET): Satellite network

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Problem: a packet from Network A cannot pass to Network C.
           Each network has its own packet format, addressing, error handling.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Previous approach: design one perfect network.
  Cerf+Kahn's insight: design a protocol that works ACROSS networks,
                       without requiring any network to change.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
DESIGN PRINCIPLES:
  ──────────────────
  1. No central control. Any network can join.
  2. Each network operates independently (no internal changes required).
  3. Best-effort delivery. Routers don't remember packets.
  4. "Black boxes" (later called routers/gateways) connect networks.
  5. Endpoints handle reliability (not the network).
  6. No global addressing — a single address space.
  7. No assumptions about the underlying network type.
```

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### TCP/IP Architecture

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin
Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
APPLICATION LAYER
  ─────────────────
  HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SSH, TLS
  Application defines message format.
  TCP/IP is transport — it doesn't care what's in the payload.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
TRANSPORT LAYER
  ───────────────
  TCP: Transmission Control Protocol
    - Reliable, ordered byte stream
    - Connection-oriented (3-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
    - Error detection + retransmission
    - Flow control (receiver advertises window size)
    - Congestion control (slow start, AIMD)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
UDP: User Datagram Protocol (added later)
    - Unreliable, unordered
    - No handshake, no retransmission
    - Low overhead (games, video streaming, DNS)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
INTERNET LAYER
  ──────────────
  IP: Internet Protocol
    - Best-effort packet delivery
    - 32-bit addresses (IPv4) / 128-bit addresses (IPv6)
    - Fragmentation and reassembly
    - TTL (Time to Live — prevents infinite loops)
    - Routing: each router forwards based on destination IP

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
LINK LAYER
  ──────────
  Ethernet, WiFi, fiber, etc.
  IP doesn't care — "any packet network" was the design goal.
  IP packets are carried inside whatever the physical network uses.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
THE KEY INSIGHT: end-to-end principle
  ──────────────────────────────────────
  Put complexity at the endpoints, not in the network.
  The network delivers packets. Period.
  Reliability, ordering, encryption — the application's problem.
  This is why TCP/IP supports VoIP, HTTP, BitTorrent, WebRTC
  without any changes to the network infrastructure.
```

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **IP addressing** (Cerf's specific contribution): The 32-bit IPv4 address space (4.3 billion addresses) was designed when the internet had ~100 nodes. By the mid-1990s, address exhaustion was visible. IPv6 (128-bit, 2^128 addresses — essentially unlimited) was standardized in 1998. IPv6 adoption is still incomplete in 2025, 25+ years later.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **The end-to-end principle** (Saltzer, Reed, Clark, 1984 — formalizing Cerf+Kahn's design): functions that can be implemented correctly only with application participation should not be implemented in the network. This principle is why the internet is general-purpose: adding a new protocol requires no changes to routers — only to endpoints. It is also why internet "neutrality" debates matter: edge-added features (content inspection, QoS prioritization) violate end-to-end.

sections.text: ## Tim Berners-Lee (1955–present)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### Bio Snapshot

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: British computer scientist. Oxford (physics). CERN from 1980. Invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989. Founded W3C in 1994. Now at MIT and Oxford. Knighted 2004. Never patented the Web — gave it away freely, a decision that shaped the open internet. Most recently advocating for the Solid decentralized web project.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### The Web Proposal

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: In March 1989, Berners-Lee submitted a proposal to his CERN management: "Information Management: A Proposal." His manager Mike Sendall wrote on it: "Vague but exciting."

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: The problem: CERN employed thousands of researchers who came and went. Each brought their own information systems. When they left, institutional knowledge left with them. Berners-Lee wanted a system where information could be linked and accessed without a central database controller.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin
Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
URI / URL — Uniform Resource Identifier / Locator
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A universal naming scheme for any resource.
  http://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
scheme://host[:port]/path?query#fragment
  http://     — protocol
  info.cern.ch — hostname (resolved via DNS)
  /hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html — path to resource

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Critical: the namespace is globally distributed.
  No central registry controls what URLs exist under a domain.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
HTTP — HyperText Transfer Protocol
  ────────────────────────────────────
  Request-response protocol.
  Stateless: each request independent.
  Verbs: GET, POST (originally); later PUT, DELETE, PATCH.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
GET /hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html HTTP/1.0
  Host: info.cern.ch

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
  Content-Type: text/html
  [body follows]

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Statelessness is a design choice (not a limitation):
  Scales horizontally — any server can handle any request.
  Session state managed by cookies (Netscape, 1994) or tokens.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
HTML — HyperText Markup Language
  ──────────────────────────────────
  Markup language for documents with links.
  Derived from SGML.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: link text The href attribute is the hypertext — the link to another document.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
HTML was intentionally simple: easy to parse, easy to write,
  graceful degradation (unknown tags ignored).
  This permissiveness led to decades of browser quirks.
```

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
**What Berners-Lee did NOT invent**:
- The internet (Cerf+Kahn, 1974)
- Hypertext (the concept: Bush 1945, Nelson 1965, Engelbart 1968)
- Packet switching (Baran, Davies, independently 1960s)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **What he did**: Combined URL + HTTP + HTML into a practical, deployed system running at CERN in December 1991. And gave it away without patents.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### The Gift to the World

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: Berners-Lee convinced CERN not to patent the Web in 1993. The technology entered the public domain. Had it been patented:

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
```
COUNTERFACTUAL: PATENTED WEB
==============================

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Every web server → license fee
  Every browser → license fee
  Every web page → potentially licensed content

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
The web would likely have developed as fragmented
  proprietary systems, similar to CompuServe, AOL, MSN
  — walled gardens with incompatible protocols.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
The open web's economic value:
    Estimated at $1–2 trillion/year globally (Deloitte, 2012).
    All of e-commerce, all of search advertising, all of SaaS.
    Berners-Lee captured essentially none of this.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Compare: Qualcomm's CDMA patents earn ~$7 billion/year.
           Berners-Lee's HTTP patents: $0.
```

sections.text: ## Marc Andreessen (1971–present)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### Bio Snapshot

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: Iowa native. Illinois (computer science). National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at University of Illinois. Co-wrote Mosaic browser with Eric Bina (1993). Co-founded Netscape (1994). Co-founded Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) VC firm (2009). Board member at Meta, HP, others.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### Mosaic and the Web's Popularization

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin
Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Before Mosaic:
    Web browsers: text-only. Lynx.
    Images: separate windows, separate downloads.
    Installation: complex. Unix command line.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Mosaic innovations:
    Inline images — images embedded in pages alongside text.
    Single-click links (not type-a-URL).
    Simple installation on Mac and Windows (not just Unix).
    Support for multiple protocols: HTTP, FTP, Gopher, NNTP.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Effect:
    Web usage grew 341,634% in 1993.
    A technical curiosity became a mass medium.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
Andreessen's design decision: allow inline images by default.
  Berners-Lee and others argued images should be separate.
  Andreessen's position won — visual web, not document web.
  This decision determined the consumer internet's character.
```

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **Netscape Navigator**: Andreessen and Jim Clark founded Mosaic Communications, renamed Netscape. Navigator was the first commercial web browser. The Netscape IPO in August 1995 — the company had no profits — validated the internet as an investment category and triggered the dot-com boom.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: Netscape's other contributions: JavaScript (Brendan Eich, 1995 — designed in 10 days), SSL/TLS (encrypted web connections), cookies (session state management). All still foundational to the web.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **The browser wars**: Microsoft responded by shipping Internet Explorer bundled with Windows 95, then 98. By 1999 IE had ~95% market share. Netscape's core technology was open-sourced as Mozilla in 1998. Firefox (2004) emerged from Mozilla and began taking share back. Eventually: Chrome (Google, 2008) dominated.

sections.text: ## Larry Page (1973–present) and Sergey Brin (1973–present)

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### Bio Snapshot

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **Page**: Michigan (computer engineering). Stanford PhD (withdrew to run Google). Former Google CEO. Now Alphabet CEO/board.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **Brin**: Maryland (math + CS). Stanford PhD (withdrew). Pioneered data mining for thesis work. Now works on special projects at Alphabet.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: Met at Stanford in 1995. Google founded 1998. IPO 2004.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ### PageRank

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **The problem with 1990s web search**: Search engines (AltaVista, Excite, Lycos) ranked results by keyword frequency in the page's text. This was easily gamed and produced low-quality results.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
```
THE PAGERANK ALGORITHM
========================

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
INSIGHT: A link from page A to page B is a vote for B.
           But not all votes are equal.
           A vote from an authoritative page (one that has many votes)
           counts more than a vote from an obscure page.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
FORMULATION:
    Let PR(A) = PageRank of page A.
    Pages that link to A: p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ.
    Let L(pᵢ) = number of outgoing links from page pᵢ.
    d = damping factor (typically 0.85).

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: PR(A) = (1 - d) + d × Σᵢ (PR(pᵢ) / L(pᵢ))

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
INTERPRETATION:
    Model a random surfer who:
    - With probability (1-d): jumps to any page at random (teleportation).
    - With probability d: follows a random link from current page.
    PR(A) = fraction of time the random surfer spends on A.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
COMPUTATION:
    Iterative. Start with PR = 1/N for all pages.
    Apply formula repeatedly until convergence.
    The web graph has ~50 billion pages → distributed computation needed.
    This was Google's MapReduce application before MapReduce was named.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
WHY IT WORKS:
    Gaming keyword frequency: easy.
    Gaming the link graph: hard. You need real pages to link to you.
    Authoritative pages (Wikipedia, NYT, .gov) have high PR.
    Their links transfer authority.
    Spam pages have few legitimate inbound links → low PR → buried.
```

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
**The infrastructure gap**: PageRank required ranking all pages in the web graph before showing any results. AltaVista was already struggling with the scale of the web. Page and Brin built a custom infrastructure:
- Crawlers to download the entire web
- Storage system for the crawled pages and link graph
- Distributed computation to run PageRank across the graph
- Fast index serving for query time

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: This infrastructure work became the foundation for MapReduce (2004), BigTable (2006), and the Google File System (2003) — papers that drove the "big data" era.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: **Google's business model**: PageRank gave relevance. The business model came from AdWords (2000) — text ads shown alongside search results, priced by cost-per-click. This model (relevance + targeted advertising) generated more revenue than anyone anticipated and funded Google's broader infrastructure ambitions.

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text: ## Comparison Table

metadata.title: Internet and Web Pioneers - Cerf, Kahn, Berners-Lee, Andreessen, Page, Brin

sections.text:
| Figure | Key Contribution | Year | Impact |
|--------|-----------------|------|--------|
| Cerf + Kahn | TCP/IP protocol | 1974 | The internet's plumbing |
| Berners-Lee | HTTP + HTML + URL (WWW) | 1989–1991 | The Web as application layer on the internet |
| Andreessen | Mosaic browser | 1993 | Web goes visual, goes mainstream |
| Page + Brin | PageRank, Google | 1998 | Web becomes findable; search as infrastructure |
